claim: Stomatal closure to fungal chitin is conferred by the major PRRs for chitin recognition, LYK5 and CERK1.
source: Here, we show that stomatal closure to fungal chitin is conferred by the major PRRs for chitin recognition, LYK5 and CERK1, the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase PBL27, and the SLAH3 anion channel.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that cerk1 and lyk5 mutants showed no closure of stomata in response to chitin treatment (Figure 1A).

claim: Stomatal closure to fungal chitin is conferred by the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase PBL27.
source: Here, we show that stomatal closure to fungal chitin is conferred by the major PRRs for chitin recognition, LYK5 and CERK1, the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase PBL27, and the SLAH3 anion channel.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that pbl27 mutants showed no closure to chitin (Figure 1B).

claim: Stomatal closure to fungal chitin is conferred by the SLAH3 anion channel.
source: Here, we show that stomatal closure to fungal chitin is conferred by the major PRRs for chitin recognition, LYK5 and CERK1, the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase PBL27, and the SLAH3 anion channel.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that slah3 mutants failed to close stomata in response to chitin (Figure 1C).

claim: PBL27 has the capacity to phosphorylate SLAH3.
source: PBL27 has the capacity to phosphorylate SLAH3, of which S127 and S189 are required to activate SLAH3.
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assays showing PBL27 trans-phosphorylates SLAH3-N and SLAH3-C (Figure 2C, 2D).

claim: S127 and S189 of SLAH3 are required to activate SLAH3.
source: PBL27 has the capacity to phosphorylate SLAH3, of which S127 and S189 are required to activate SLAH3.
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments showing that S127A mutation abrogates PBL27 activation of SLAH3 (Figure 3F) and S189A compromises CERK1-dependent full activation (Figure 3G).

claim: Full activation of SLAH3 entails CERK1, depending on PBL27.
source: Full activation of the channel entails CERK1, depending on PBL27.
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments showing SLAH3-mediated anion current amplitudes were strongly increased in the presence of CERK1 co-injection when activated by PBL27 (Figure 3C).

claim: Both S127 and S189 residues of SLAH3 are required for chitin-induced stomatal closure.
source: Importantly, both S127 and S189 residues of SLAH3 are required for chitin-induced stomatal closure and anti-fungal immunity at the whole leaf level.
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements showing plants expressing S127A and S189A variants failed to close stomata in response to chitin (Figure 4B, 4C).

claim: Both S127 and S189 residues of SLAH3 are required for anti-fungal immunity at the whole leaf level.
source: Importantly, both S127 and S189 residues of SLAH3 are required for chitin-induced stomatal closure and anti-fungal immunity at the whole leaf level.
evidence: Supported by lesion diameter analysis showing slah3 mutants and complementation lines expressing S127A and S189A developed larger disease lesions from B. cinerea (Figure 5A).

claim: SLAH3 activation by PBL27 is independent of ABA-induced SLAH3 activation.
source: Our results demonstrate a short signal transduction module from MAMP recognition to anion channel activation, and independent of ABA-induced SLAH3 activation.
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments showing PBL27-mediated activation of SLAH3 was not suppressed upon co-injecting the protein phosphatase ABI1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Single null cerk1 mutant plants showed no closure of stomata in response to chitin treatment.
source: Single null cerk1 and lyk5 mutant plants showed no closure of stomata in response to chitin treatment, whilst lyk2, lyk3, and lyk4 behaved like wild-type plants (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements in mutants (Figure 1A).

claim: Single null lyk5 mutant plants showed no closure of stomata in response to chitin treatment.
source: Single null cerk1 and lyk5 mutant plants showed no closure of stomata in response to chitin treatment, whilst lyk2, lyk3, and lyk4 behaved like wild-type plants (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements in mutants (Figure 1A).

claim: lyk2, lyk3, and lyk4 mutants behaved like wild-type plants in stomatal closure response to chitin.
source: Single null cerk1 and lyk5 mutant plants showed no closure of stomata in response to chitin treatment, whilst lyk2, lyk3, and lyk4 behaved like wild-type plants (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements in mutants (Figure 1A).

claim: LYK5 represents the major chitin receptor and induces chitin signalling through complex formation with CERK1.
source: This is in agreement with LYK5 representing the major chitin receptor and inducing chitin signalling through complex formation with CERK1 (Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cao et al., 2014.

claim: PBL27 is preferentially phosphorylated by CERK1 signalling.
source: Given that PBL27 is preferentially phosphorylated by CERK1 signalling (Shinya et al., 2014), consistently stomata of pbl27 mutants showed no closure to chitin either (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shinya et al., 2014.

claim: Stomata of pbl27 mutants showed no closure to chitin.
source: Given that PBL27 is preferentially phosphorylated by CERK1 signalling (Shinya et al., 2014), consistently stomata of pbl27 mutants showed no closure to chitin either (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements (Figure 1B).

claim: Transgenic expression of CERK1-GFP fusion variants restored chitin-induced stomatal closure in cerk1 mutants.
source: Transgenic expression of respective C-terminally tagged green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusion variants restored chitin-induced stomatal closure in cerk1, lyk5 and pbl27 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements in transgenic lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Transgenic expression of LYK5-GFP fusion variants restored chitin-induced stomatal closure in lyk5 mutants.
source: Transgenic expression of respective C-terminally tagged green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusion variants restored chitin-induced stomatal closure in cerk1, lyk5 and pbl27 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements in transgenic lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Transgenic expression of PBL27-GFP fusion variants restored chitin-induced stomatal closure in pbl27 mutants.
source: Transgenic expression of respective C-terminally tagged green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusion variants restored chitin-induced stomatal closure in cerk1, lyk5 and pbl27 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements in transgenic lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Single slah3 mutants failed to close stomata in response to chitin.
source: Unexpectedly, single slah3 mutants, which are sensitive to pattern-induced stomatal closure (Zheng et al., 2018; Guzel Deger et al., 2015), failed to close stomata in response to the fungal MAMP (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements (Figure 1C).

claim: Single slac1 mutants exhibited wild type-like chitin-induced stomatal closure.
source: Single slac1 mutants exhibited wild type-like chitin-induced stomatal closure (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements (Figure 1C).

claim: Stomata of slah3 mutant showed intermediate levels of closure to chitosan.
source: Yet, in this case, stomata of slah3 mutant showed intermediate levels of closure, being not significantly different to stomatal apertures in chitosan-stimulated wild type guard cells and unstimulated guard cells of slah3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by chitosan current ejection experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: CERK1 binds both chitin and chitosan with a preference for long-chain oligosaccharides.
source: CERK1 binds both chitin and chitosan with a preference for long-chain oligosaccharides (Petutschnig et al., 2010), suggesting that it is a major receptor in chitin-induced closure of stomata.
evidence: Supported by citation to Petutschnig et al., 2010.

claim: SLAH3 interacts with PBL27 in N. benthamiana.
source: After transient expression of SLAH3 together with CERK1 and PBL27 in N. benthamiana, we observed a clear fluorescent signal of SLAH3-YFPn and PBL27-YFPc but not SLAH3-YFPn and CERK1D441V-YFPc (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by BiFC experiments showing fluorescent signal of SLAH3-YFPn and PBL27-YFPc (Figure 2A).

claim: SLAH3 does not interact with CERK1 kinase dead variant in N. benthamiana.
source: After transient expression of SLAH3 together with CERK1 and PBL27 in N. benthamiana, we observed a clear fluorescent signal of SLAH3-YFPn and PBL27-YFPc but not SLAH3-YFPn and CERK1D441V-YFPc (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by BiFC experiments showing no fluorescent signal of SLAH3-YFPn and CERK1D441V-YFPc (Figure 2A).

claim: CERK1 kinase dead is competent to interact with LYK5.
source: Of note, we used kinase dead (KD) transient expression of CERK1D441V-YFPc, which is competent to interact with LYK5-YFPn (Figure 2A), as wild type CERK1 promoted cell death in N. benthamiana.
evidence: Supported by BiFC experiments showing interaction between CERK1D441V-YFPc and LYK5-YFPn (Figure 2A).

claim: Co-expression of SLAH3 with BIK1 did not reconstitute a detectable fluorescent signal.
source: Importantly, co-expression of SLAH3-YFPn with BIK1-YFPc, also competent to associate with CERK1 (Zhang et al., 2010), did not reconstitute a detectable fluorescent signal (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by BiFC experiments showing no fluorescent signal (Figure 2A).

claim: BIK1 is competent to associate with CERK1.
source: Importantly, co-expression of SLAH3-YFPn with BIK1-YFPc, also competent to associate with CERK1 (Zhang et al., 2010), did not reconstitute a detectable fluorescent signal (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: Co-expression of BIK1 with RBOHD generated fluorescent signals.
source: By contrast, co-expression of BIK1-YFPc but not PBL27-YFPc with YFPn-RBOHD generated fluorescent signals (Figure 2A), consistent with the notion that BIK1 signalling activates the RBOHD-mediated ROS burst to flagellin and that single pbl27 mutants are not compromised in chitin-induced ROS (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Shinya et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by BiFC experiments showing fluorescent signals (Figure 2A).

claim: Co-expression of PBL27 with RBOHD did not generate fluorescent signals.
source: By contrast, co-expression of BIK1-YFPc but not PBL27-YFPc with YFPn-RBOHD generated fluorescent signals (Figure 2A), consistent with the notion that BIK1 signalling activates the RBOHD-mediated ROS burst to flagellin and that single pbl27 mutants are not compromised in chitin-induced ROS (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Shinya et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by BiFC experiments showing no fluorescent signals (Figure 2A).

claim: BIK1 signalling activates the RBOHD-mediated ROS burst to flagellin.
source: By contrast, co-expression of BIK1-YFPc but not PBL27-YFPc with YFPn-RBOHD generated fluorescent signals (Figure 2A), consistent with the notion that BIK1 signalling activates the RBOHD-mediated ROS burst to flagellin and that single pbl27 mutants are not compromised in chitin-induced ROS (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Shinya et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kadota et al., 2014 and Li et al., 2014.

claim: Single pbl27 mutants are not compromised in chitin-induced ROS.
source: By contrast, co-expression of BIK1-YFPc but not PBL27-YFPc with YFPn-RBOHD generated fluorescent signals (Figure 2A), consistent with the notion that BIK1 signalling activates the RBOHD-mediated ROS burst to flagellin and that single pbl27 mutants are not compromised in chitin-induced ROS (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Shinya et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shinya et al., 2014.

claim: SLAH3-FLAG associates with PBL27-T7 in N. benthamiana.
source: To independently confirm the PBL27-SLAH3 interaction in N. benthamiana, we immuno-precipitated SLAH3-FLAG and observed that it associated with PBL27-T7 but not BIK1-T7, and that the association was independent of chitin stimulation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2B).

claim: SLAH3-FLAG does not associate with BIK1-T7 in N. benthamiana.
source: To independently confirm the PBL27-SLAH3 interaction in N. benthamiana, we immuno-precipitated SLAH3-FLAG and observed that it associated with PBL27-T7 but not BIK1-T7, and that the association was independent of chitin stimulation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2B).

claim: The association between SLAH3 and PBL27 is independent of chitin stimulation.
source: To independently confirm the PBL27-SLAH3 interaction in N. benthamiana, we immuno-precipitated SLAH3-FLAG and observed that it associated with PBL27-T7 but not BIK1-T7, and that the association was independent of chitin stimulation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with and without chitin treatment (Figure 2B).

claim: SLAH3 exists in a complex with PBL27 in a chitin-independent manner.
source: Together, these results show that SLAH3 exists in a complex with PBL27 in a chitin-independent manner.
evidence: Supported by BiFC and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2A, 2B).

claim: PBL27 trans-phosphorylates SLAH3-N in vitro.
source: In vitro phosphorylation experiments using N- and C-terminal domains of SLAH3 indicated that PBL27, but not its kinase dead variant PBL27K112E, trans-phosphorylated both the N-and C-terminal domain of SLAH3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assays (Figure 2C).

claim: PBL27 trans-phosphorylates SLAH3-C in vitro.
source: In vitro phosphorylation experiments using N- and C-terminal domains of SLAH3 indicated that PBL27, but not its kinase dead variant PBL27K112E, trans-phosphorylated both the N-and C-terminal domain of SLAH3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assays (Figure 2C).

claim: PBL27 kinase dead variant does not trans-phosphorylate SLAH3-N or SLAH3-C in vitro.
source: In vitro phosphorylation experiments using N- and C-terminal domains of SLAH3 indicated that PBL27, but not its kinase dead variant PBL27K112E, trans-phosphorylated both the N-and C-terminal domain of SLAH3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assays (Figure 2C).

claim: A weaker in vitro trans-phosphorylation was observed for SLAH3-C compared with SLAH3-N.
source: Of note, a weaker in vitro trans-phosphorylation could be observed for SLAH3-C compared with SLAH3-N (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assays (Figure 2C).

claim: PBL27 directly interacts with SLAH3.
source: The finding that PBL27 phosphorylates SLAH3 in vitro also provides evidence for a direct interaction between these two proteins, which is consistent with our BiFC and co-immunoprecipitation results (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Inferred from in vitro phosphorylation experiments and supported by BiFC and co-immunoprecipitation results (Figure 2A, 2B, 2C).

claim: SLAH3-N and SLAH3-C are phosphorylated more strongly when incubated with PBL27-HA purified from chitin-treated plants.
source: Both SLAH3-N and SLAH3-C were clearly phosphorylated when incubated with PBL27-HA, which was significantly stronger when PBL27-HA was purified from chitin-treated plants (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assays using PBL27-HA from chitin-treated and untreated plants (Figure 2D).

claim: PBL27 is able to trans-phosphorylate SLAH3-N and SLAH3-C depending on chitin stimulation.
source: This revealed that PBL27 is able to trans-phosphorylate SLAH3-N and SLAH3-C depending on chitin stimulation.
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assays using PBL27-HA from chitin-treated and untreated plants (Figure 2D).

claim: Elicitation with chitin led to SLAH3 phosphorylation in vivo.
source: Elicitation with chitin led to SLAH3 phosphorylation, as indicated by a band shift, which can be reversed upon phosphatase treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by Phos-tag SDS-PAGE analysis (Figure 2E).

claim: SLAH3 phosphorylation status can be regulated by PBL27 and depends on chitin stimulation.
source: Together, our in vitro and in vivo data provide evidence that SLAH3 phosphorylation status can be regulated by PBL27 and depends on chitin stimulation.
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assays and Phos-tag SDS-PAGE analysis (Figure 2D, 2E).

claim: SLAH3 remained silent when injected into Xenopus oocytes alone.
source: In two-electrode voltage clamp (TEVC) experiments SLAH3 remained silent when it was injected into Xenopus oocytes alone (Figure 3A) (Geiger et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by TEVC experiments (Figure 3A) and citation to Geiger et al., 2011.

claim: Co-injection of SLAH3 with PBL27 generated macroscopic S-type anion currents.
source: By contrast, co-injection with PBL27 generated macroscopic S-type anion currents (Figure 3A), with current amplitudes of 8 µA similar to SLAH3 activated by calcium-insensitive CPK21ΔEF or CBL1/CIPK23 (Figure 3B) (Maierhofer et al., 2014a; Geiger et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by TEVC experiments (Figure 3A, 3B).

claim: PBL27 is sufficient to trigger SLAH3-mediated anion transport independent of ABA signalling.
source: This suggests that PBL27 is sufficient to trigger SLAH3-mediated anion transport independent of ABA signalling (Geiger et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from ABI1 co-injection experiments and supported by citation to Geiger et al., 2010.

claim: PBL27 did not activate SLAC1.
source: Here it should be noted that PBL27 did not activate SLAC1, unlike OST1 and CBL1/CIPK23 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and which is consistent with wild type-like stomatal closure in slac1 mutants (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: OST1 activates SLAC1.
source: Here it should be noted that PBL27 did not activate SLAC1, unlike OST1 and CBL1/CIPK23 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and which is consistent with wild type-like stomatal closure in slac1 mutants (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: CBL1/CIPK23 activates SLAC1.
source: Here it should be noted that PBL27 did not activate SLAC1, unlike OST1 and CBL1/CIPK23 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and which is consistent with wild type-like stomatal closure in slac1 mutants (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: SLAH3-mediated anion current amplitudes were strongly increased in the presence of CERK1 co-injection when activated by PBL27.
source: SLAH3-mediated anion current amplitudes were strongly increased in the presence of CERK1 but not LYK5 co-injection, when activated by PBL27 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3C).

claim: SLAH3-mediated anion current amplitudes were not increased in the presence of LYK5 co-injection when activated by PBL27.
source: SLAH3-mediated anion current amplitudes were strongly increased in the presence of CERK1 but not LYK5 co-injection, when activated by PBL27 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3C).

claim: When LYK5 and CERK1 were co-injected without PBL27, SLAH3 remained silent.
source: When LYK5 and CERK1 were co-injected without PBL27, SLAH3 remained silent (Figure 3C), corresponding with SLAH3 interaction with PBL27 but not CERK1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3C).

claim: Only signalling-competent CERK1 amplified PBL27-mediated SLAH3 activation.
source: Consistent with the finding that PBL27 is phosphorylated by CERK1 (Shinya et al., 2014), only signalling-competent CERK1 amplified PBL27-mediated SLAH3 activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D) and citation to Shinya et al., 2014.

claim: Activation of SLAH3 by PBL27 was dependent on its kinase activity.
source: Activation of SLAH3 by PBL27 was dependent on its kinase activity (Figure 3B), which was also necessary for amplified SLAH3 activation by CERK1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments using kinase dead PBL27 (Figure 3B).

claim: PBL27 kinase activity was necessary for amplified SLAH3 activation by CERK1.
source: Activation of SLAH3 by PBL27 was dependent on its kinase activity (Figure 3B), which was also necessary for amplified SLAH3 activation by CERK1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).

claim: The phosphorylation status of PBL27 correlates with the activation of SLAH3.
source: This suggests that the phosphorylation status of PBL27 correlates with the activation of SLAH3 and is in agreement with enhanced phosphorylation of SLAH3 when PBL27 was purified from chitin-stimulated cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Inferred from oocyte experiments and supported by in vitro kinase assays (Figure 2D, Figure 3).

claim: Co-injection with CERK1 inhibited PBL1 activation of SLAH3.
source: Unexpectedly, co-injection with CERK1 inhibited PBL1 activation of SLAH3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).

claim: PBL27 is the primary kinase that directly phosphorylates SLAH3 for the release of anions.
source: We conclude that PBL27 is the primary kinase that directly phosphorylates SLAH3 for the release of anions and functions in an activation status-dependent manner regulated by CERK1.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing PBL27 phosphorylates and activates SLAH3, and CERK1 amplifies this activation.

claim: PBL27 functions in an activation status-dependent manner regulated by CERK1.
source: We conclude that PBL27 is the primary kinase that directly phosphorylates SLAH3 for the release of anions and functions in an activation status-dependent manner regulated by CERK1.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing CERK1 amplifies PBL27-mediated SLAH3 activation.

claim: SLAH3 was phosphorylated at S127, S189, and S601 by PBL27 in vitro.
source: We discovered that SLAH3 was phosphorylated at three sites by PBL27: S127 and S189 at SLAH3-N and S601 at SLAH3-C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and C).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B and C).

claim: Single phospho-mimic mutations of S127, S189 and S601 did not auto-activate SLAH3.
source: In oocytes, injection of single phospho-mimic mutations of S127, S189 and S601 (S127D, S189D and S601D) did not auto-activate SLAH3 and had no impact on PBL27 activation of SLAH3 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3D).

claim: The double mutant S127D/S189D was constitutive active.
source: However, remarkably, the double mutant S127D/S189D, but neither S127D/S601D nor S189D/S601D, was constitutive active (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3E).

claim: S127D/S601D was not constitutive active.
source: However, remarkably, the double mutant S127D/S189D, but neither S127D/S601D nor S189D/S601D, was constitutive active (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3E).

claim: S189D/S601D was not constitutive active.
source: However, remarkably, the double mutant S127D/S189D, but neither S127D/S601D nor S189D/S601D, was constitutive active (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3E).

claim: Co-expression of S127D/S189D with PBL27 did not result in a further increase in anion currents.
source: Interestingly, co-expression of S127D/S189D with PBL27 did not result in a further increase in anion currents whereas S127D/S601D and S189D/S601D could still be activated by PBL27 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3E).

claim: S127D/S601D and S189D/S601D could still be activated by PBL27.
source: Interestingly, co-expression of S127D/S189D with PBL27 did not result in a further increase in anion currents whereas S127D/S601D and S189D/S601D could still be activated by PBL27 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3E).

claim: The phosphorylation status of both S127 and S189 is critical for SLAH3 channel opening.
source: These results provide evidence that the phosphorylation status of both S127 and S189 is critical for SLAH3 channel opening.
evidence: Inferred from oocyte experiments showing S127D/S189D double mutant is constitutive active (Figure 3E).

claim: PBL27 activation of SLAH3 is abrogated by S127A.
source: Importantly, we observed that PBL27 activation of SLAH3 is abrogated by S127A, but not S189 and S601 (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3F).

claim: PBL27 activation of SLAH3 is not abrogated by S189A.
source: Importantly, we observed that PBL27 activation of SLAH3 is abrogated by S127A, but not S189 and S601 (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3F).

claim: PBL27 activation of SLAH3 is not abrogated by S601A.
source: Importantly, we observed that PBL27 activation of SLAH3 is abrogated by S127A, but not S189 and S601 (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3F).

claim: S127A did not affect the activation of SLAH3 by CPK21ΔEF and CBL1/CIPK23.
source: We also found that S127A did not affect the activation of SLAH3 by other kinases such as CPK21ΔEF and CBL1/CIPK23 or by the heteromerization with the silent anion channel subunit SLAH1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) (Cubero-Font et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).

claim: S127A did not affect the activation of SLAH3 by heteromerization with SLAH1.
source: We also found that S127A did not affect the activation of SLAH3 by other kinases such as CPK21ΔEF and CBL1/CIPK23 or by the heteromerization with the silent anion channel subunit SLAH1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) (Cubero-Font et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) and citation to Cubero-Font et al., 2016.

claim: PBL27 regulates SLAH3 activation through phosphorylation of S127, a site not required for CPK21 and CBL1/CIPK23 activation of SLAH3.
source: These results demonstrate that PBL27 regulates SLAH3 activation through phosphorylation of S127, a site not required for CPK21 and CBL1/CIPK23 activation of SLAH3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).

claim: S127 phosphorylation is required for SLAH3 activation by PBL27 but not sufficient by itself to induce anion transport.
source: However, whilst S127 phosphorylation is required for SLAH3 activation by PBL27, it is not sufficient by itself to induce anion transport (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments showing S127D alone does not auto-activate SLAH3 (Figure 3D).

claim: S127 can only auto-activate SLAH3 in the context of additional S189 phospho-mimicry.
source: It can only auto-activate SLAH3 in the context of additional S189 phospho-mimicry (Figure 3E), and thus suggests a functional link between these two residues in SLAH3 channel opening.
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments showing S127D/S189D double mutant is constitutive active (Figure 3E).

claim: The S189A mutation resulted in constitutive activation of SLAH3.
source: Surprisingly, the S189A instead of the S189D mutation resulted in constitutive activation of SLAH3 (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3D, 3F).

claim: The S189A auto-activation could not be further elevated by co-injection of PBL27, CIPK23/CBL1, or SLAH1.
source: The S189A auto-activation could not be further elevated by co-injection of PBL27 or other anion channel activating components like CIPK23/CBL1 or SLAH1 (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).

claim: CERK1-mediated amplification of SLAH3 activation by PBL27 is compromised in the S189A constitutive active variant of SLAH3.
source: However, CERK1-mediated amplification of SLAH3 activation by PBL27 is compromised in the S189A constitutive active variant of SLAH3 (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3G).

claim: PBL27 phosphorylation of S127 activates SLAH3 but full opening of the SLAH3 channel additionally requires PBL27 phosphorylation of S189, in a CERK1-dependent manner.
source: Thus, it seems that PBL27 phosphorylation of S127 activates SLAH3 but full opening of the SLAH3 channel additionally requires PBL27 phosphorylation of S189, in a CERK1-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from oocyte experiments showing S127A abrogates PBL27 activation and S189A compromises CERK1-dependent amplification (Figure 3F, 3G).

claim: S601 is not involved in phosphorylation-dependent or -independent activation of SLAH3.
source: S601 seems not to be involved in phosphorylation-dependent or -independent activation of SLAH3, since the mutant S601A could be either activated by PBL27 (Figure 3F) or by CPK21ΔEF, CIPK23/CBL1 and SLAH1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).

claim: Transgenic slah3 plants expressing wild-type SLAH3 showed chitin-induced stomatal closure.
source: Transgenic slah3 plants expressing wild-type SLAH3 showed chitin-induced stomatal closure (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements (Figure 4A).

claim: Plants expressing the S127A variant failed to close stomata in response to chitin.
source: By contrast, plants expressing the S127A and S189A variants failed to close stomata in response to chitin, similar to slah3 mutants (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements (Figure 4B).

claim: Plants expressing the S189A variant failed to close stomata in response to chitin.
source: By contrast, plants expressing the S127A and S189A variants failed to close stomata in response to chitin, similar to slah3 mutants (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements (Figure 4C).

claim: Plants expressing the S601A SLAH3 variant behaved wild type-like in chitin-induced stomatal closure.
source: As expected from oocyte experiments (Figure 3F), plants expressing the S601A SLAH3 variant behaved wild type-like (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by stomatal aperture measurements (Figure 4D).

claim: Mutant slah3 plants developed larger disease lesions from B. cinerea three days post inoculation relative to Col-0.
source: Lesion diameter analysis revealed that relative to Col-0 and complementation lines expressing SLAH3 wild type, mutant slah3 plants and complementation lines expressing S127A and S189A, but not S601A, developed larger disease lesions three days post inoculation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by lesion diameter measurements (Figure 5A).

claim: Complementation lines expressing S127A developed larger disease lesions from B. cinerea three days post inoculation relative to Col-0.
source: Lesion diameter analysis revealed that relative to Col-0 and complementation lines expressing SLAH3 wild type, mutant slah3 plants and complementation lines expressing S127A and S189A, but not S601A, developed larger disease lesions three days post inoculation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by lesion diameter measurements (Figure 5A).

claim: Complementation lines expressing S189A developed larger disease lesions from B. cinerea three days post inoculation relative to Col-0.
source: Lesion diameter analysis revealed that relative to Col-0 and complementation lines expressing SLAH3 wild type, mutant slah3 plants and complementation lines expressing S127A and S189A, but not S601A, developed larger disease lesions three days post inoculation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by lesion diameter measurements (Figure 5A).

claim: Complementation lines expressing S601A did not develop larger disease lesions from B. cinerea three days post inoculation relative to Col-0.
source: Lesion diameter analysis revealed that relative to Col-0 and complementation lines expressing SLAH3 wild type, mutant slah3 plants and complementation lines expressing S127A and S189A, but not S601A, developed larger disease lesions three days post inoculation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by lesion diameter measurements (Figure 5A).

claim: slah3 mutants showed wild type-like chitin-induced ROS burst.
source: Notably, slah3 mutants were not generally immune-compromised, since we observed wild type-like chitin-induced ROS burst and ethylene production (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by ROS production measurements (Figure 5B).

claim: slah3 mutants showed wild type-like chitin-induced ethylene production.
source: Notably, slah3 mutants were not generally immune-compromised, since we observed wild type-like chitin-induced ROS burst and ethylene production (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by ethylene accumulation measurements (Figure 5C).

claim: The chitin-induced ROS burst was not altered in pbl27 mutants.
source: We also found that the chitin-induced ROS burst was not altered in pbl27 mutants (Figure 5D), consistent with previous studies (Shinya et al., 2014) and that PBL27 showed no interaction with RBOHD (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by ROS production measurements (Figure 5D) and citation to Shinya et al., 2014.

claim: Examination of B. cinerea infection in pbl27 revealed no significant differences compared with wild type.
source: Examination of B. cinerea infection in pbl27 revealed no significant differences compared with wild type (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by lesion diameter measurements (Figure 5E).

claim: S127 and S189 are important for SLAH3 function in resistance to B. cinerea.
source: Our infection studies revealed that S127 and S189 are important for SLAH3 function in resistance to B. cinerea.
evidence: Supported by lesion diameter measurements showing S127A and S189A lines developed larger lesions (Figure 5A).

claim: The same phospho-sites regulate chitin-induced stomatal closure and anti-fungal immunity at the whole leaf level.
source: Thus, the same phospho-sites regulate chitin-induced stomatal closure and anti-fungal immunity at the whole leaf level.
evidence: Inferred from stomatal closure and infection assays showing S127 and S189 are required for both processes (Figure 4, Figure 5A).

claim: Many agronomical important pathogens penetrate plant tissues directly through the epidermis or via stomata.
source: Many agronomical important pathogens penetrate plant tissues directly through the epidermis or via stomata (Grimmer et al., 2012; Faulkner and Robatzek, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grimmer et al., 2012 and Faulkner and Robatzek, 2012.

claim: Fungal pathogens are the causal agents of devastating diseases such as rust fungi.
source: These include fungal pathogens that are the causal agents of devastating diseases such as rust fungi (Fones et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2016; Bebber and Gurr, 2015; Shafiei et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fones et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2016; Bebber and Gurr, 2015; Shafiei et al., 2007.

claim: Epidermal cells are highly immunomodulatory to oligosaccharides of fungal chitin.
source: To defend fungal infection at the level of penetration, epidermal cells are highly immunomodulatory to oligosaccharides of fungal chitin, a microbe-associated molecular pattern (MAMP) present across fungal families (Faulkner and Robatzek, 2012; McLachlan et al., 2014; Koers et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Faulkner and Robatzek, 2012; McLachlan et al., 2014; Koers et al., 2011.

claim: Chitin is a microbe-associated molecular pattern (MAMP) present across fungal families.
source: To defend fungal infection at the level of penetration, epidermal cells are highly immunomodulatory to oligosaccharides of fungal chitin, a microbe-associated molecular pattern (MAMP) present across fungal families (Faulkner and Robatzek, 2012; McLachlan et al., 2014; Koers et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations and established knowledge.

claim: In Arabidopsis, perception of chitin is mediated at the cell surface by three related pattern recognition receptors (PRRs).
source: In Arabidopsis, perception of chitin is mediated at the cell surface by three related pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) (Boutrot and Zipfel, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boutrot and Zipfel, 2017.

claim: CERK1 and LYK5 encode single-pass transmembrane receptor kinases.
source: CHITIN ELICITOR RECEPTOR KINASE 1 (CERK1) and LYSINE MOTIF (LysM) RECEPTOR KINASE 5 (LYK5) encode single-pass transmembrane receptor kinases (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: LYM2 encodes a receptor-like protein predominantly present at plasmodesmal membranes and specifically involved in cell-to-cell signalling.
source: LysM-domain-containing GLYCOSYLPHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL (GPI)-anchored protein 2 (LYM2) encodes a receptor-like protein predominantly present at plasmodesmal membranes and specifically involved in cell-to-cell signalling (Faulkner et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Faulkner et al., 2013.

claim: The middle LysM domain of CERK1 was shown to bind directly to chitin oligomers.
source: Their ectodomains consist of three LysM domains, of which in CERK1 the middle LysM domain was shown to bind directly to chitin oligomers (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: LYK5 is the major chitin receptor in Arabidopsis, binding chitin oligomers with higher affinity than CERK1.
source: Recent data demonstrate that LYK5 is the major chitin receptor in Arabidopsis, binding chitin oligomers with higher affinity than CERK1 (Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cao et al., 2014.

claim: Upon chitin binding, LYK5 forms a complex with CERK1 leading to signal generation.
source: Upon chitin binding, LYK5 forms a complex with CERK1 leading to signal generation, which depends on CERK1 autophosphorylation at specific threonine and tyrosine residues and dephosphorylation by the CERK1-INTERACTING PROTEIN PHOSPHATASE 1 (CIPP1) phosphatase (Cao et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2018; Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2018; Suzuki et al., 2016.

claim: Signal generation from LYK5-CERK1 complex depends on CERK1 autophosphorylation at specific threonine and tyrosine residues.
source: Upon chitin binding, LYK5 forms a complex with CERK1 leading to signal generation, which depends on CERK1 autophosphorylation at specific threonine and tyrosine residues and dephosphorylation by the CERK1-INTERACTING PROTEIN PHOSPHATASE 1 (CIPP1) phosphatase (Cao et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2018; Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2018; Suzuki et al., 2016.

claim: Signal generation from LYK5-CERK1 complex depends on dephosphorylation by CIPP1 phosphatase.
source: Upon chitin binding, LYK5 forms a complex with CERK1 leading to signal generation, which depends on CERK1 autophosphorylation at specific threonine and tyrosine residues and dephosphorylation by the CERK1-INTERACTING PROTEIN PHOSPHATASE 1 (CIPP1) phosphatase (Cao et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2018; Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cao et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2018; Suzuki et al., 2016.

claim: A key event of PRR signalling is the phosphorylation of receptor complex-associated RECEPTOR-LIKE CYTOPLASMIC KINASES (RLCKs).
source: A key event of PRR signalling is the phosphorylation of receptor complex-associated RECEPTOR-LIKE CYTOPLASMIC KINASES (RLCKs), which induces the release of the RLCKs from the PRR complex and activation of downstream substrates (Rao et al., 2018; Bi et al., 2018; Yamada et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rao et al., 2018; Bi et al., 2018; Yamada et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: Phosphorylation of RLCKs induces the release of the RLCKs from the PRR complex and activation of downstream substrates.
source: A key event of PRR signalling is the phosphorylation of receptor complex-associated RECEPTOR-LIKE CYTOPLASMIC KINASES (RLCKs), which induces the release of the RLCKs from the PRR complex and activation of downstream substrates (Rao et al., 2018; Bi et al., 2018; Yamada et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rao et al., 2018; Bi et al., 2018; Yamada et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: BIK1 and PBL1 induce defence signalling downstream of CERK1.
source: BOTRYTIS-INDUCED KINASE 1 (BIK1) and the closely related PROBABLE SERINE/THREONINE-PROTEIN KINASE-LIKE 1 (PBL1) of the VII-8 subgroup induce defence signalling downstream of CERK1, the bacterial MAMP receptors FLAGELLIN SENSING 2 (FLS2) and EF-TU RECEPTOR (EFR), and the danger receptors PEP1 RECEPTOR KINASEs (PEPR) 1 and PEPR2 (Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013.

claim: BIK1 and PBL1 induce defence signalling downstream of FLS2 and EFR.
source: BOTRYTIS-INDUCED KINASE 1 (BIK1) and the closely related PROBABLE SERINE/THREONINE-PROTEIN KINASE-LIKE 1 (PBL1) of the VII-8 subgroup induce defence signalling downstream of CERK1, the bacterial MAMP receptors FLAGELLIN SENSING 2 (FLS2) and EF-TU RECEPTOR (EFR), and the danger receptors PEP1 RECEPTOR KINASEs (PEPR) 1 and PEPR2 (Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013.

claim: BIK1 and PBL1 induce defence signalling downstream of PEPR1 and PEPR2.
source: BOTRYTIS-INDUCED KINASE 1 (BIK1) and the closely related PROBABLE SERINE/THREONINE-PROTEIN KINASE-LIKE 1 (PBL1) of the VII-8 subgroup induce defence signalling downstream of CERK1, the bacterial MAMP receptors FLAGELLIN SENSING 2 (FLS2) and EF-TU RECEPTOR (EFR), and the danger receptors PEP1 RECEPTOR KINASEs (PEPR) 1 and PEPR2 (Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013.

claim: CERK1-dependent chitin signalling is shared with members of the RLCK VII-4 subgroup and PBL27 belonging to the VII-1 subgroup.
source: CERK1-dependent chitin signalling is shared with members of the RLCK VII-4 subgroup and PBL27 belonging to the VII-1 subgroup (Rao et al., 2018; Yamada et al., 2016), highlighting that subfamily VII RLCKs have both redundant and specific roles (Rao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rao et al., 2018 and Yamada et al., 2016.

claim: Subfamily VII RLCKs have both redundant and specific roles.
source: CERK1-dependent chitin signalling is shared with members of the RLCK VII-4 subgroup and PBL27 belonging to the VII-1 subgroup (Rao et al., 2018; Yamada et al., 2016), highlighting that subfamily VII RLCKs have both redundant and specific roles (Rao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rao et al., 2018.

claim: Higher order mutants of VII-1, VII-4 and VII-8 subgroup members are all compromised in the chitin-induced burst of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Consistently, higher order mutants of VII-1, VII-4 and VII-8 subgroup members are all compromised in the chitin-induced burst of reactive oxygen species (ROS) while showing different response signatures depending on the type of MAMP and defence reaction (Rao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rao et al., 2018.

claim: PBL27 is a direct substrate of CERK1.
source: Being a direct substrate of CERK1, initial studies suggest that pbl27 mutants were not defective in chitin-induced ROS burst but MITOGEN -ACTIVATED PROTEIN KINASES 3/6 (MPK3/6) signalling and callose deposition (Yamada et al., 2016; Shinya et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yamada et al., 2016 and Shinya et al., 2014.

claim: Initial studies suggest that pbl27 mutants were not defective in chitin-induced ROS burst but MPK3/6 signalling and callose deposition.
source: Being a direct substrate of CERK1, initial studies suggest that pbl27 mutants were not defective in chitin-induced ROS burst but MITOGEN -ACTIVATED PROTEIN KINASES 3/6 (MPK3/6) signalling and callose deposition (Yamada et al., 2016; Shinya et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yamada et al., 2016 and Shinya et al., 2014.

claim: PBL27 phosphorylates MAPKKK5 in a CERK1-dependent manner, resulting in the dissociation of MAPKKK5 from PBL27 and activation of MKK4 and MKK5.
source: PBL27 was shown to phosphorylate MAPKKK5 in a CERK1-dependent manner, resulting in the dissociation of MAPKKK5 from PBL27 and activation of MKK4 and MKK5, upstream kinases of the MAPK signalling cascade (Yamada et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yamada et al., 2016.

claim: Chitin-triggered MAPK activation was not compromised in single pbl27 and higher order rlck vii-1 mutants.
source: However, these findings are recently challenged, since chitin-triggered MAPK activation was not compromised in single pbl27 and higher order rlck vii-1 mutants (Rao et al., 2018), suggesting that more research is required.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rao et al., 2018.

claim: Subgroup VII-4 members are involved in activation of MPK3/6 by chitin, yet not immune signalling by bacterial flagellin.
source: Instead, subgroup VII-4 members are involved in activation of MPK3/6 by chitin, yet not immune signalling by bacterial flagellin (Ranf et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ranf et al., 2014.

claim: BIK1 and PBL1 are required for flagellin-induced ROS production but not MAPK activation.
source: On the other hand, BIK1 and PBL1 are required for flagellin-induced ROS production but not MAPK activation (Zhang et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2010 and Li et al., 2014.

claim: MAMP perception results in the closure of stomata.
source: MAMP perception results in the closure of stomata, pores formed by a guard cell pair, and thereby promotes plant tissue surface immunity (McLachlan et al., 2014; Melotto et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to McLachlan et al., 2014 and Melotto et al., 2006.

claim: Infectious pathogens secrete effectors which function to inhibit closure of stomata and to induce stomatal opening.
source: As a counterstrategy and demonstrating the importance of stomatal closure, infectious pathogens secrete effectors, which function to inhibit closure of stomata and to induce stomatal opening, or lock stomata in the wide open state by fungal-produced fusicoccin (McLachlan et al., 2014; Lozano-Durán et al., 2014; Melotto et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to McLachlan et al., 2014; Lozano-Durán et al., 2014; Melotto et al., 2006.

claim: Guard cells have been well established as a single cell model system and used to dissect both immune- and ABA-signalling.
source: Reducing the complexity of whole plant/organ systems with different cell types, guard cells have been well established as a single cell model system and used to dissect both immune- and ABA-signalling (Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Qi et al., 2017.

claim: Stomatal apertures are controlled by cell volume changes triggered upon ion fluxes.
source: Stomatal apertures are controlled by cell volume changes triggered upon ion fluxes (McLachlan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to McLachlan et al., 2014 and established knowledge.

claim: Stomatal closure to bacterial flagellin requires activation of S-type anion channels mediated by SLAC1 and SLAH3.
source: Stomatal closure to bacterial flagellin requires activation of S-type anion channels mediated by the SLOW ANION CHANNEL-ASSOCIATED 1 (SLAC1), a weak rectifying anion channel present at the plasma membrane of guard cells, and closely related SLAC1 HOMOLOG 3 (SLAH3) (Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Montillet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guzel Deger et al., 2015 and Montillet et al., 2013.

claim: Exposure to chitin oligosaccharides and chitosan reduce stomatal apertures.
source: Exposure to chitin oligosaccharides (herein referred to as chitin) and chitosan, a deacetylated derivative of chitin, reduce stomatal apertures (Bourdais et al., 2019; Klüsener et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bourdais et al., 2019 and Klüsener et al., 2002.

claim: Chitosan stimulates S-type anion channels.
source: Evidence suggest that chitosan stimulates S-type anion channels (Koers et al., 2011), but the molecular components involved in channel activation and thus promoting stomatal closure to chitin and derivatives remain elusive.
evidence: Supported by citation to Koers et al., 2011.

claim: In abiotic stress signalling, SLAC1 is activated by OST1, which involves S120 phosphorylation of the SLAC1 N-terminus and is independent of elevated cytoplasmic calcium.
source: In abiotic stress signalling, SLAC1 is activated by OPEN STOMATA 1 (OST1), a SUCROSE NON-FERMENTING 1 (SNF1)-related protein kinase (SnRK), which involves S120 phosphorylation of the SLAC1 N-terminus and is independent of elevated cytoplasmic calcium (Geiger et al., 2010; Vahisalu et al., 2010; Geiger et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geiger et al., 2010; Vahisalu et al., 2010; Geiger et al., 2009.

claim: Elevation of cytosolic calcium activates S-type anion channels.
source: Yet, elevation of cytosolic calcium also activates S-type anion channels (Stange et al., 2010; Schroeder and Hagiwara, 1989), consistent with the findings that CALCIUM-DEPENDENT PROTEIN KINASE 3 (CPK3) and CPK21 activate SLAC1 (Geiger et al., 2010; Scherzer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stange et al., 2010; Schroeder and Hagiwara, 1989; Geiger et al., 2010; Scherzer et al., 2012.

claim: CPK3 and CPK21 activate SLAC1.
source: Yet, elevation of cytosolic calcium also activates S-type anion channels (Stange et al., 2010; Schroeder and Hagiwara, 1989), consistent with the findings that CALCIUM-DEPENDENT PROTEIN KINASE 3 (CPK3) and CPK21 activate SLAC1 (Geiger et al., 2010; Scherzer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geiger et al., 2010 and Scherzer et al., 2012.

claim: CPK6 and CPK23 activate SLAC1 largely independent of cytosolic calcium elevation.
source: CPK6 and CPK23 also appear to activate SLAC1 but largely independent of cytosolic calcium elevation (Geiger et al., 2010; Scherzer et al., 2012), which involves S59 phosphorylation at the SLAC1 N-terminus (Brandt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geiger et al., 2010; Scherzer et al., 2012; Brandt et al., 2012.

claim: CPK6 and CPK23 activation of SLAC1 involves S59 phosphorylation at the SLAC1 N-terminus.
source: CPK6 and CPK23 also appear to activate SLAC1 but largely independent of cytosolic calcium elevation (Geiger et al., 2010; Scherzer et al., 2012), which involves S59 phosphorylation at the SLAC1 N-terminus (Brandt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brandt et al., 2012.

claim: CBL1, CBL9, and CIPK23 are capable of SLAC1 activation through a phosphorylated residue distinct from OST1 phosphorylation.
source: Moreover, calcium sensitive CALCINEURIN B-LIKE 1 (CBL1) and CBL9 together with CBL-INTERACTING PROTEIN KINASE 23 (CIPK23) are capable of SLAC1 activation, through a phosphorylated residue distinct from OST1 phosphorylation (Maierhofer et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maierhofer et al., 2014a.

claim: Different kinases regulate SLAC1 activity at distinct phosphorylation sites.
source: This demonstrates that different kinases regulate SLAC1 activity at distinct phosphorylation sites.
evidence: Inferred from multiple studies showing different kinases phosphorylate different sites on SLAC1.

claim: SLAH3 is only activated upon co-expression of CPKs and CBL/CIPKs but not by OST1.
source: SLAH3 is only activated upon co-expression of CPKs and CBL/CIPKs but not by OST1 (Maierhofer et al., 2014a; Geiger et al., 2011), suggesting a different mode of regulation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Maierhofer et al., 2014a and Geiger et al., 2011.

claim: Previous studies suggested several kinases in guard cell signalling downstream of FLS2, including BIK1, MPK3/6 and OST1.
source: Previous studies suggested several kinases in guard cell signalling downstream of FLS2, including BIK1, MPK3/6 and OST1 (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Montillet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Montillet et al., 2013.

claim: The Arabidopsis LYK5-CERK1-PBL27 receptor complex is responsible for chitin-induced stomatal closure and anti-fungal immunity.
source: Here, we identify that the Arabidopsis LYK5-CERK1-PBL27 receptor complex is responsible for chitin-induced stomatal closure and anti-fungal immunity.
evidence: Supported by genetic and biochemical experiments (Figure 1, Figure 5).

claim: PBL27 directly interacts with and phosphorylates SLAH3.
source: Using biochemical and molecular approaches, we show that PBL27 directly interacts with and phosphorylates SLAH3, consistent with SLAH3 phosphorylation induced by chitin.
evidence: Supported by BiFC, co-immunoprecipitation, and in vitro kinase assays (Figure 2).

claim: SLAH3 phosphorylation is induced by chitin.
source: Using biochemical and molecular approaches, we show that PBL27 directly interacts with and phosphorylates SLAH3, consistent with SLAH3 phosphorylation induced by chitin.
evidence: Supported by Phos-tag SDS-PAGE analysis (Figure 2E).

claim: Both S127 and S189 phospho-sites are critical for PBL27-mediated activation of SLAH3.
source: Both phospho-sites are critical for PBL27-mediated activation of SLAH3 and revealing a role for S189 in CERK1-dependent amplification of SLAH3 opening.
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments (Figure 3).

claim: S189 has a role in CERK1-dependent amplification of SLAH3 opening.
source: Both phospho-sites are critical for PBL27-mediated activation of SLAH3 and revealing a role for S189 in CERK1-dependent amplification of SLAH3 opening.
evidence: Supported by oocyte experiments showing S189A compromises CERK1-dependent amplification (Figure 3G).

claim: An S-type anion channel is a novel target of RLCKs with relevance to immune defences.
source: Taken together, our data identified an S-type anion channel as a novel target of RLCKs with relevance to immune defences.
evidence: Inferred from all experimental data showing PBL27 activates SLAH3 for immune responses.

claim: Chitin binding activates the LYK5-CERK1 receptors, inducing auto-phosphorylation and trans-phosphorylation events.
source: In such a model, chitin binding activates the LYK5-CERK1 receptors, inducing auto-phosphorylation and trans-phosphorylation events (Couto and Zipfel, 2016), which result in the phosphorylation and activation of PBL27 (Shinya et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Couto and Zipfel, 2016 and Shinya et al., 2014.

claim: Chitin binding results in the phosphorylation and activation of PBL27.
source: In such a model, chitin binding activates the LYK5-CERK1 receptors, inducing auto-phosphorylation and trans-phosphorylation events (Couto and Zipfel, 2016), which result in the phosphorylation and activation of PBL27 (Shinya et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shinya et al., 2014.

claim: PBL27 pre-exists in a complex with SLAH3 independent of chitin stimulus.
source: As PBL27 pre-exists in a complex with SLAH3 independent of chitin stimulus (Figure 2A,B), activated PBL27 enhanced the phosphorylation of the SLAH3 N-terminus (Figure 2D), which fully opens SLAH3 to release anions (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by BiFC and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2A, 2B).

claim: Activated PBL27 enhanced the phosphorylation of the SLAH3 N-terminus.
source: As PBL27 pre-exists in a complex with SLAH3 independent of chitin stimulus (Figure 2A,B), activated PBL27 enhanced the phosphorylation of the SLAH3 N-terminus (Figure 2D), which fully opens SLAH3 to release anions (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assays (Figure 2D).

claim: Full activation of SLAH3 appears to be required for chitin-induced stomatal closure and resistance to B. cinerea infection.
source: Full activation of SLAH3 appears to be required for chitin-induced stomatal closure and resistance to B. cinerea infection (Figure 3F and G, Figure 4, Figure 5A): S127 is a phospho-site required for SLAH3 activation by kinase-active PBL27, and S189 represents a phospho-site, which is sensitive to amplifying SLAH3 opening by CERK1-activated PBL27 (Figure 3G).
evidence: Inferred from stomatal closure and infection assays (Figure 3F, 3G, Figure 4, Figure 5A).

claim: Stomatal closure induced by FLS2 and PEPR1/2 signalling relies on both SLAH3 and SLAC1.
source: Stomatal closure induced by FLS2 and PEPR1/2 signalling relies on both SLAH3 and SLAC1, and requires BIK1 for activation of anion currents in response to PEPR1/2 signalling (Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guzel Deger et al., 2015 and Zheng et al., 2018.

claim: BIK1 is required for activation of anion currents in response to PEPR1/2 signalling.
source: Stomatal closure induced by FLS2 and PEPR1/2 signalling relies on both SLAH3 and SLAC1, and requires BIK1 for activation of anion currents in response to PEPR1/2 signalling (Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guzel Deger et al., 2015 and Zheng et al., 2018.

claim: Different PRRs integrate different RLCK VII members for distinct signalling outputs.
source: Being directly associated with PRRs (Yamada et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010), it seems that different PRRs integrate different RLCK VII members for distinct signalling outputs (Rao et al., 2018), i.e. FLS2-activated BIK1 phosphorylates RBOHD to produce ROS (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from multiple studies and supported by citations to Yamada et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Rao et al., 2018; Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014.

claim: FLS2-activated BIK1 phosphorylates RBOHD to produce ROS.
source: Being directly associated with PRRs (Yamada et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010), it seems that different PRRs integrate different RLCK VII members for distinct signalling outputs (Rao et al., 2018), i.e. FLS2-activated BIK1 phosphorylates RBOHD to produce ROS (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kadota et al., 2014 and Li et al., 2014.

claim: This work identifies a phospho-regulatory pathway that directly links PRR complexes with S-type anion transportation in a specific and signalling-dependent manner.

claim: CERK1 functions in LYM1 and LYM3 perception of bacterial peptidoglycan (PGN).
source: Since CERK1 also functions in LYM1 and LYM3 perception of bacterial peptidoglycan (PGN) (Willmann et al., 2011), it will be interesting to explore whether PGN induces stomatal closure through SLAH3 activation by PBL27 or PBL1, thereby promoting anti-bacterial immunity at the level of tissue invasion.
evidence: Supported by citation to Willmann et al., 2011.
